q: How much fuel can a dye house save by recovering heat from hot drain water?
title: Dye house drain heat recovery: fuel saved
short: Heat recovered = flow x 4.186 kJ per kg per degree C x (drain temperature minus fresh water temperature) x exchanger effectiveness. With 200 kL a day of 70 degree C drain heating 28 degree C fresh water at 60% effectiveness, that is about 21 GJ a day, or about 30 GJ of boiler fuel.

ul: Hot drain you can capture: keep hot dyeing and soaping drains apart from cold rinses. Mixed drains are cooler and give back less.
The temperature gap between the drain and incoming water.
Exchanger effectiveness: plate exchangers recover more but foul with lint; shell and tube or self-cleaning designs suit dirty drains. Effectiveness falls as fouling builds.
Timing: drains come in bursts. A hot drain tank and a warm water tank let you use the heat when the next bath fills.

sections.h: From recovered heat to fuel and CO2
p: Fuel saved = heat recovered / boiler efficiency, provided that fresh water would otherwise have been heated with steam to at least the preheated temperature. CO2 avoided = fuel energy x the fuel's IPCC 2006 factor per GJ. BEE Guide Book 2, in its waste heat recovery chapter, uses the same heat balance.

ul: Pump power for the drain and fresh water circuits: subtract kWh x 0.710 (FY 2024-25 grid factor) kg CO2.
Lint and fibre filters need daily cleaning; a fouled exchanger loses effectiveness.
Preheated water used where cold water would do saves nothing.

sections.h: A side benefit at the ETP
p: Cooler effluent suits the biological stage of an ETP, which works poorly when wastewater is too hot. Treat this as a side benefit, not part of the fuel saving.

example.title: Worked example: 200 kL a day of hot drain
lines: Hot drain 200 kL a day at 70 degrees C; fresh water 28 degrees C at an equal flow; effectiveness 60%
Heat recovered: 0.60 x 2,00,000 kg x 4.186 x (70 minus 28) = 21,097,440 kJ, about 21.10 GJ a day; fresh water leaves at about 28 + 0.6 x 42 = 53 degrees C
Boiler at 70% efficiency: 21.10 / 0.70 = 30.14 GJ of fuel a day
Coal at 94.6 kg CO2 per GJ: 30.14 x 94.6 = 2,851 kg CO2 a day
Pumps: 15 kW x 20 h = 300 kWh x 0.710 = 213 kg CO2 a day, so net 2,638 kg a day
300 working days: about 9,042 GJ of fuel and 791 t CO2 net
example.note: Flows, effectiveness, boiler efficiency and pump power are illustrative. Use measured drain flows and temperatures. The fuel line stays in GJ because the per-kg coal factor of 2.42 assumes coal of about 25.6 MJ per kg; weaker coal emits less per kg.

senseible: Senseible reads boiler fuel invoices and electricity bills, so the fuel saved and the extra pump power both show in the monthly Scope 1 and 2 records. Drain flows and temperatures come from your own measurements.
